title: Circadian Rhythm
summary: Your body's internal 24-hour clock that regulates sleep, hormones, digestion, and mood.
body: Every cell in your body runs on a roughly 24-hour cycle called the circadian rhythm. This internal clock is synchronized primarily by light exposure — specifically, morning sunlight signals your brain to stop producing melatonin and start producing cortisol, waking you up and sharpening focus. Evening darkness triggers the reverse. Disrupting this rhythm (through late-night screens, irregular sleep times, or night shifts) has been linked to metabolic dysfunction, mood disorders, and impaired immune function. Aligning your lifestyle with your circadian rhythm is one of the highest-leverage health interventions available.
keyPoints: Morning light within 30 min of waking anchors your rhythm
Cortisol peaks naturally 30-45 min after waking
Core body temperature drop signals sleep onset
Meal timing influences metabolic circadian clocks

title: Melatonin
summary: The hormone that signals darkness and prepares your body for sleep — not a sedative, but a timing signal.
body: Melatonin is produced by the pineal gland in response to darkness. It doesn't make you sleepy directly — it signals your body that night has arrived, triggering a cascade of physiological changes: core body temperature drops, blood pressure lowers, and sleep pressure builds. Bright light, especially blue light from screens, suppresses melatonin production even after sunset. Supplemental melatonin is most effective in low doses (0.3–0.5mg) for jet lag or circadian shifting — high doses (5–10mg) common in supplements may cause next-day grogginess and are far above physiological levels.
keyPoints: Produced in darkness, suppressed by light
Low doses (0.3mg) are more physiologically accurate than typical 5–10mg supplements
Blue light from screens suppresses melatonin for hours
Peaks around 2–3am in most people

title: Sleep Pressure (Adenosine)
summary: The biochemical buildup of tiredness that makes sleep feel irresistible after a long day.
body: As you stay awake, a molecule called adenosine accumulates in your brain — this buildup is literally what you experience as tiredness. The longer you're awake, the more adenosine builds, and the stronger the pressure to sleep. During sleep, adenosine is cleared. Caffeine works by blocking adenosine receptors — it doesn't remove adenosine, it just prevents you from feeling it. This is why caffeine 'crashes' occur when it wears off and all the accumulated adenosine suddenly signals at once. Napping before adenosine builds too high (before 2pm) can relieve pressure without disrupting nighttime sleep.
keyPoints: Adenosine builds during waking hours and clears during sleep
Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors rather than reducing adenosine
Sleep deprivation creates adenosine debt
Naps before 2pm can help without disrupting night sleep

title: Cortisol Awakening Response
summary: The natural morning cortisol surge that wakes you up, sharpens focus, and sets your energy for the day.
body: Within 30–45 minutes of waking, cortisol naturally spikes to its daily peak — this is called the Cortisol Awakening Response (CAR). This surge mobilizes energy, sharpens alertness, and primes your immune system for the day. Viewing bright light (ideally sunlight) immediately after waking amplifies this response. Delaying caffeine intake by 90–120 minutes after waking allows the CAR to complete naturally before adenosine blocking begins, resulting in more sustained energy and a less pronounced afternoon crash. Chronic stress blunts the CAR, which manifests as morning grogginess and low motivation.
keyPoints: Cortisol peaks 30–45 min after waking
Morning light amplifies the CAR
Delaying caffeine 90 min optimizes natural energy
Blunted CAR is a marker of chronic stress

title: Inflammation
summary: The body's protective response to injury or threat — healing when acute, harmful when chronic.
body: Inflammation is your immune system's first response to injury, infection, or stress. Acute inflammation (the redness and swelling after a cut) is protective and resolves within days. Chronic low-grade inflammation — which can persist for years without obvious symptoms — is now recognized as a root driver of most modern diseases: heart disease, type 2 diabetes, Alzheimer's, depression, and cancer. Key drivers of chronic inflammation include processed foods, seed oils, sleep deprivation, chronic stress, sedentary behavior, gut dysbiosis, and environmental toxins. Anti-inflammatory lifestyle factors include omega-3 fats, polyphenol-rich foods, sleep, movement, and stress management.
keyPoints: Acute inflammation is protective; chronic inflammation is damaging
Ultra-processed foods are a major driver of systemic inflammation
CRP and IL-6 are common inflammatory biomarkers
Sleep deprivation dramatically increases inflammatory markers overnight

title: Gut Microbiome
summary: The trillions of microorganisms living in your digestive tract that influence digestion, immunity, mood, and more.
body: Your gut contains approximately 38 trillion microorganisms — bacteria, viruses, fungi, and archaea — collectively called the microbiome. This ecosystem influences digestion and nutrient absorption, produces neurotransmitters like serotonin (90% of which is made in the gut), trains your immune system, and communicates directly with your brain via the vagus nerve (the gut-brain axis). Diversity is the key marker of a healthy microbiome. Modern diets, antibiotics, and stress reduce microbial diversity. Fiber from diverse plant foods is the primary fuel for beneficial bacteria — different fibers feed different species, which is why eating 30+ different plants per week is now a leading recommendation.
keyPoints: 90% of serotonin is produced in the gut
Diversity of species = diversity of plant foods eaten
The vagus nerve connects gut bacteria to brain directly
Antibiotics can disrupt the microbiome for months to years

title: Autophagy
summary: Your cells' self-cleaning process — breaking down damaged components and recycling them for energy and repair.
body: Autophagy (from Greek: 'self-eating') is a cellular recycling process where cells identify and break down damaged proteins, dysfunctional organelles, and pathogens, then repurpose the components. It's a critical longevity mechanism — the accumulation of cellular debris is implicated in aging, neurodegeneration, and cancer. Autophagy is suppressed by insulin and mTOR (activated by eating, especially protein and carbohydrates) and upregulated by fasting, caloric restriction, and exercise. The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2016 was awarded for discovering autophagy regulation. Practically, this means periods without eating (16+ hours for meaningful autophagy) allow cells to clean house.
keyPoints: Suppressed by eating (especially protein and carbs), activated by fasting
Upregulated after 16–24 hours of fasting
Exercise also stimulates autophagy independent of fasting
Critical for preventing neurodegeneration and cancer

title: mTOR
summary: The master growth switch — activated by nutrients and exercise, it drives muscle building but suppresses cellular cleanup.
body: mTOR (mechanistic Target Of Rapamycin) is a central nutrient-sensing pathway that acts as a growth switch. When activated by amino acids (especially leucine), insulin, and growth factors, mTOR drives protein synthesis, cell growth, and muscle building. When inhibited (during fasting or caloric restriction), autophagy increases and cells shift into maintenance mode. The tension between mTOR activation (needed for muscle growth) and mTOR inhibition (needed for longevity through autophagy) is one of the central challenges in longevity optimization. Time-restricted eating allows strategic mTOR activation (around training) while preserving periods of mTOR inhibition for cellular repair.
keyPoints: mTOR activation = growth mode (muscle building)
mTOR inhibition = repair mode (autophagy)
Leucine is the most potent amino acid activator
Rapamycin (an mTOR inhibitor) extends lifespan in animal models

title: HRV (Heart Rate Variability)
summary: The variation in time between heartbeats — a window into your autonomic nervous system's recovery and resilience.
body: Heart Rate Variability (HRV) measures the millisecond-level variation between successive heartbeats. Counterintuitively, more variation is better — high HRV indicates your autonomic nervous system can rapidly shift between sympathetic (fight-or-flight) and parasympathetic (rest-and-digest) states, reflecting adaptability and recovery capacity. Low HRV signals accumulated stress, overtraining, illness, or poor sleep. HRV is influenced by sleep quality, alcohol, training load, stress, and nutrition. Morning HRV (measured immediately on waking) is the most useful data point for training readiness. Wearables like WHOOP, Garmin, and Oura track HRV and provide recovery scores based on it.
keyPoints: Higher HRV = better recovery and resilience
Even one drink of alcohol significantly lowers HRV
Morning HRV is the most actionable measurement
Trends over weeks matter more than single data points

title: Zone 2 Cardio
summary: Low-intensity aerobic training that builds metabolic health, mitochondrial density, and fat-burning capacity.
body: Zone 2 refers to an exercise intensity where you can hold a conversation but feel slightly breathless — roughly 60–70% of maximum heart rate. At this intensity, your body primarily burns fat through aerobic metabolism. Training in Zone 2 for extended periods (45–90 minutes) builds mitochondrial density, improves insulin sensitivity, enhances fat oxidation capacity, and develops the aerobic base that supports all higher-intensity performance. Researchers like Iñigo San Millán and Peter Attia advocate for 3–4 hours of Zone 2 per week as a cornerstone of longevity. The 'talk test' is a simple way to gauge it: if you can speak in full sentences but wouldn't want to sing, you're in Zone 2.
keyPoints: ~60–70% of max heart rate
Primary fuel source is fat (fatty acid oxidation)
Builds mitochondrial density over time
3–4 hours/week is the longevity recommendation

title: VO2 Max
summary: The maximum rate at which your body can use oxygen — the single strongest predictor of longevity in all of medicine.
body: VO2 max is the maximum volume of oxygen your body can utilize per minute per kilogram of body weight during intense exercise. It reflects the combined efficiency of your lungs, heart, blood, and muscles at oxygen delivery and utilization. Studies consistently show VO2 max is the single strongest predictor of all-cause mortality — people in the top quartile for VO2 max live significantly longer than those in the bottom quartile, with a risk reduction larger than quitting smoking. It is trainable at any age. High-intensity interval training (HIIT) and Zone 5 efforts (near-maximal efforts of 3–8 minutes) are the most effective stimuli for improving VO2 max.
keyPoints: Strongest single predictor of longevity
Bottom quartile = 5x higher mortality risk vs top quartile
Trainable at any age, including in the elderly
HIIT is the most efficient training method to increase it

title: Insulin Sensitivity
summary: How efficiently your cells respond to insulin — the foundation of metabolic health and energy regulation.
body: Insulin is the hormone that signals cells to take up glucose from the bloodstream. Insulin sensitivity describes how effectively cells respond to this signal. High insulin sensitivity means cells respond readily to small amounts of insulin — glucose is cleared quickly and efficiently. Insulin resistance (the opposite) means cells have become sluggish to insulin signals, forcing the pancreas to produce more and more insulin to achieve the same effect. Insulin resistance precedes type 2 diabetes by years or decades and is linked to obesity, PCOS, cardiovascular disease, and cognitive decline. Exercise, sleep, and reducing processed carbohydrates are the most effective interventions.
keyPoints: Insulin resistance precedes type 2 diabetes by 10–15 years
Muscle is the primary site of glucose disposal
Exercise acutely improves insulin sensitivity for 24–48 hours
Fasting insulin is a better early marker than fasting glucose

title: Mitochondria
summary: The energy-producing organelles in your cells — their health determines your energy, resilience, and longevity.
body: Mitochondria are organelles found in nearly every cell, responsible for producing ATP (adenosine triphosphate) — the energy currency of life. They operate as tiny power plants, converting oxygen and nutrients into usable energy through a process called oxidative phosphorylation. Mitochondrial health is central to longevity: mitochondrial dysfunction underlies aging, neurodegeneration, metabolic disease, and chronic fatigue. Key factors that support mitochondrial health include aerobic exercise (especially Zone 2), cold exposure, intermittent fasting, CoQ10, NAD+ precursors (NMN/NR), and red/infrared light. Mitochondria have their own DNA, inherited exclusively through the maternal line.
keyPoints: Primary producers of ATP (cellular energy)
Mitochondrial dysfunction is central to aging
Zone 2 training is the most potent stimulus for new mitochondria (biogenesis)
NAD+ declines with age and is critical for mitochondrial function

title: NAD+
summary: A critical coenzyme that powers cellular energy and DNA repair — and declines dramatically with age.
body: NAD+ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) is a coenzyme found in every cell, essential for energy metabolism, DNA repair, and the activation of sirtuins (longevity proteins). NAD+ levels decline by approximately 50% between ages 20 and 60. This decline is implicated in mitochondrial dysfunction, reduced DNA repair capacity, and aging itself. NMN (nicotinamide mononucleotide) and NR (nicotinamide riboside) are precursors that boost NAD+ levels. Exercise, fasting, and heat exposure also naturally raise NAD+. David Sinclair's research at Harvard has been central to popularizing NAD+ precursors as longevity supplements, though human clinical evidence is still developing.
keyPoints: Declines ~50% between ages 20–60
Essential for sirtuin activation (longevity proteins)
NMN and NR are the primary supplement precursors
Exercise and fasting naturally boost NAD+

title: Cortisol
summary: The primary stress hormone — essential for survival and morning energy, harmful when chronically elevated.
body: Cortisol is a glucocorticoid hormone produced by the adrenal glands in response to stress and as part of the natural circadian rhythm. Its primary functions are mobilizing glucose for energy, reducing inflammation acutely, and suppressing non-essential functions (digestion, reproduction, immune activity) during stress. The morning cortisol surge (Cortisol Awakening Response) is healthy and adaptive. Problems arise with chronic cortisol elevation from ongoing psychological stress, sleep deprivation, or overtraining. Chronically high cortisol causes muscle breakdown, fat accumulation (especially visceral), suppressed immunity, disrupted sleep, and cognitive impairment.
keyPoints: Natural morning peak is healthy and adaptive
Chronic elevation drives visceral fat accumulation
Suppresses immune, digestive, and reproductive function when chronically high
Sleep deprivation is one of the most potent cortisol elevators

title: Vagus Nerve
summary: The main highway of your parasympathetic nervous system — connecting brain, heart, lungs, and gut.
body: The vagus nerve is the longest cranial nerve in the body, running from the brainstem through the neck, chest, and abdomen. It is the primary nerve of the parasympathetic ('rest and digest') nervous system, carrying signals between the brain and the heart, lungs, and digestive tract. Vagal tone — the functional strength of vagal activity — is a marker of resilience and recovery capacity. High vagal tone is associated with better HRV, lower inflammation, and greater emotional regulation. Vagal tone can be increased through practices including cold exposure, slow diaphragmatic breathing, humming, singing, gargling, and meditation.
keyPoints: Carries 80% of signals from gut to brain (not brain to gut)
Vagal tone correlates with HRV
Slow breathing (4–6 breaths/min) maximally activates the vagus
Cold water on the face activates the diving reflex via vagus

title: Intermittent Fasting
summary: A pattern of eating that cycles between periods of fasting and eating — not a diet, but a timing protocol.
body: Intermittent fasting (IF) refers to eating patterns that include defined fasting periods, most commonly 16:8 (16 hours fasting, 8-hour eating window) or 5:2 (normal eating 5 days, very low calorie 2 days). During the fasting state, insulin drops, fat burning increases, and cellular repair processes like autophagy are upregulated. IF can improve insulin sensitivity, support weight management, reduce inflammation, and trigger autophagy. It is not inherently superior to continuous caloric restriction for weight loss when calories are matched. Women may be more sensitive to fasting stress than men and may benefit from shorter fasting windows (12–14 hours) to avoid hormonal disruption.
keyPoints: 16:8 is the most common protocol
Benefits amplify significantly after 16–24 hours
Women may need shorter fasting windows (12–14h) to avoid hormonal disruption
Caloric restriction accounts for much of the weight loss benefit

title: Cold Exposure
summary: Deliberate exposure to cold temperatures to trigger adaptive stress responses that improve resilience and metabolism.
body: Cold exposure — through cold showers, ice baths, or cold water immersion — triggers a hormetic stress response: the body experiences a controlled stressor and adapts to become more resilient. Acute effects include a large release of norepinephrine (up to 300% increase), which improves mood, focus, and alertness. Regular cold exposure activates brown adipose tissue (BAT), increases mitochondrial density, reduces inflammation, and may improve insulin sensitivity. Timing matters: cold exposure after strength training may blunt some hypertrophy adaptations by reducing the inflammatory signal needed for muscle growth. Best used in the morning or after cardio.
keyPoints: Norepinephrine increases up to 300% with cold immersion
Activates brown fat (metabolically active fat that burns energy)
Avoid immediately post-strength training (may blunt hypertrophy)
11 minutes per week total is associated with benefits in research

title: Heat Exposure (Sauna)
summary: Regular sauna use mimics cardiovascular exercise and activates powerful heat shock proteins that protect cells.
body: Regular sauna use (particularly Finnish sauna at 80–100°C) produces cardiovascular effects comparable to moderate-intensity exercise — heart rate rises to 120–150 bpm, cardiac output increases, and blood pressure temporarily drops. Long-term, Finnish population studies show 4–7 sessions per week correlates with dramatically reduced cardiovascular mortality. Heat stress activates heat shock proteins (HSPs), which repair misfolded proteins and protect against neurodegeneration. Sauna use also increases growth hormone, improves insulin sensitivity, and enhances mood through endorphin and dynorphin release. Post-sauna, a cold plunge amplifies the norepinephrine response.
keyPoints: 4–7 sauna sessions/week linked to 40% reduction in cardiovascular mortality (Finnish study)
Heat shock proteins repair misfolded proteins
Growth hormone can spike 200–300% after sauna
Hydration is critical — you can lose 0.5–1L per session

title: Omega-3 Fatty Acids
summary: Essential anti-inflammatory fats critical for brain health, cardiovascular function, and cellular membrane integrity.
body: Omega-3 fatty acids — particularly EPA and DHA found in fatty fish and fish oil — are structural components of every cell membrane and are powerfully anti-inflammatory. EPA (eicosapentaenoic acid) primarily modulates inflammation and mood, while DHA (docosahexaenoic acid) is concentrated in the brain and retina, essential for cognitive function and neuroplasticity. The modern diet is dramatically skewed toward omega-6 fats (from seed oils), creating an inflammatory ratio. Most researchers recommend 2–4g of combined EPA+DHA daily for significant anti-inflammatory effects. The Omega-3 Index (% of EPA+DHA in red blood cell membranes) is a superior biomarker to serum levels.
keyPoints: EPA is anti-inflammatory; DHA is structural for brain and eyes
Aim for Omega-3 Index of 8–12% (most people are at 4–6%)
Algae-based DHA is the vegan equivalent
Oxidized fish oil is worse than no supplement — quality matters

title: Magnesium
summary: A mineral involved in 300+ enzymatic reactions — chronically deficient in modern populations.
body: Magnesium is a cofactor in over 300 enzymatic reactions, including ATP production, DNA synthesis, protein synthesis, and muscle/nerve function. It is the fourth most abundant mineral in the body yet chronically deficient in modern populations due to mineral-depleted soils, processed food diets, and high stress (stress depletes magnesium rapidly). Deficiency manifests as muscle cramps, poor sleep, anxiety, constipation, headaches, and fatigue. Different forms have different bioavailability and functions: magnesium glycinate and threonate are best for sleep and cognitive function; magnesium malate for energy; citrate for constipation. Most adults benefit from 300–400mg daily, ideally taken in the evening.
keyPoints: Involved in 300+ enzymatic reactions including ATP production
Stress dramatically depletes magnesium
Different forms have different targets (glycinate for sleep, threonate for brain)
Blood serum levels are a poor measure — most magnesium is intracellular

title: Vitamin D
summary: A fat-soluble hormone (not just a vitamin) essential for immunity, bone health, mood, and gene expression.
body: Vitamin D functions more like a hormone than a vitamin — it regulates the expression of over 1,000 genes. Vitamin D3 is synthesized in skin upon UVB exposure or consumed from fatty fish, egg yolks, and supplements. It is critical for calcium absorption, immune regulation, mood, muscle function, and cardiovascular health. Deficiency is endemic — an estimated 41% of adults in the US are deficient. Optimal blood levels are debated but most functional medicine practitioners target 50–80 ng/mL (125–200 nmol/L). Vitamin K2 should be taken alongside D3 to direct calcium to bones and away from arteries. Magnesium is required to activate vitamin D.
keyPoints: Regulates over 1,000 genes
41% of US adults are deficient
K2 must be taken with D3 to direct calcium properly
Magnesium is required to convert vitamin D to its active form

title: Breathwork
summary: Deliberate manipulation of breathing patterns to shift the nervous system, alter consciousness, and improve resilience.
body: Breathing is the only autonomic function you can consciously control, making it a direct lever on the autonomic nervous system. Slow, extended exhales activate the parasympathetic nervous system, reducing heart rate and stress. Fast, hyperventilating patterns (like Wim Hof or holotropic breathwork) temporarily alter blood CO2 and pH, producing altered states, adrenaline release, and potentially euphoria. Specific protocols: box breathing (4-4-4-4) for acute stress; 4-7-8 breathing for sleep onset; physiological sigh (double inhale through nose, long exhale) for rapid stress relief; resonance breathing (5-6 breaths/min) for HRV optimization.
keyPoints: Slow exhales activate parasympathetic; fast breathing activates sympathetic
Physiological sigh is the fastest way to reduce acute stress
Resonance breathing (5–6 breaths/min) maximally elevates HRV
CO2 tolerance training improves athletic performance and stress resilience

title: Polyphenols
summary: Plant compounds with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties that support the gut microbiome and longevity pathways.
body: Polyphenols are a large family of plant-derived compounds including flavonoids, resveratrol, quercetin, curcumin, and catechins. They act as antioxidants, reduce inflammation, modulate gut bacteria, and activate longevity pathways including sirtuins and AMPK. Foods richest in polyphenols include berries, dark chocolate (70%+), green tea, extra virgin olive oil, red wine, and colorful vegetables. Many polyphenols have poor bioavailability but gut bacteria convert them into more bioactive metabolites — which is why gut health matters for getting full benefit. Resveratrol (in red wine and grapes) and quercetin activate SIRT1; curcumin inhibits NF-kB (a master inflammatory regulator).
keyPoints: Berries, dark chocolate, EVOO, and green tea are top sources
Gut bacteria convert polyphenols into more bioactive forms
Curcumin needs piperine (black pepper) for absorption
Resveratrol and quercetin activate sirtuin longevity pathways

title: Hormesis
summary: The principle that low doses of stress make biological systems stronger — the foundation of exercise, fasting, and biohacking.
body: Hormesis describes the biological phenomenon where exposure to a low dose of a stressor that would be harmful at high doses actually produces a beneficial adaptive response. Exercise is the classic example: physical stress damages muscle fibers and depletes energy, triggering adaptations that make you stronger and more resilient. Fasting, cold exposure, heat stress, and even certain plant toxins (like sulforaphane from broccoli, which activates Nrf2) operate through hormetic mechanisms. The key is dose: too little produces no adaptation, the optimal dose produces maximum benefit, and too much causes harm. Recovery between stressors is essential — the adaptation happens during recovery, not during the stressor itself.
keyPoints: The dose makes the medicine — too much stress = damage
Recovery between stressors is when adaptation occurs
Sulforaphane, exercise, fasting, cold, and heat all work via hormesis
Nrf2 pathway is the master regulator of hormetic stress response

title: AMPK
summary: The cellular energy sensor that activates fat burning, autophagy, and longevity pathways when energy is low.
body: AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) is a master cellular energy sensor. When intracellular energy (ATP) is low — during fasting, caloric restriction, or intense exercise — AMPK is activated. It functions as a metabolic switch: it upregulates fatty acid oxidation (fat burning), stimulates glucose uptake, inhibits mTOR (thus promoting autophagy), activates mitochondrial biogenesis, and turns on SIRT1. AMPK is essentially the cellular signal that you are in a calorie-restricted state, triggering all the beneficial adaptations associated with fasting. Metformin (a diabetes drug used off-label for longevity) and berberine work primarily by activating AMPK. Exercise is the most potent physiological AMPK activator.
keyPoints: Activated by low energy (fasting, exercise, caloric restriction)
Inhibits mTOR and activates autophagy
Activates mitochondrial biogenesis
Metformin and berberine are AMPK activators

title: Sirtuins
summary: A family of longevity proteins that regulate aging, DNA repair, and metabolism — activated by caloric restriction and NAD+.
body: Sirtuins (SIRT1-7) are a family of NAD+-dependent enzymes that regulate gene expression, DNA repair, metabolism, and aging. They are often called 'longevity proteins' because their activity is strongly associated with extended lifespan across species. Sirtuins are activated by NAD+ (which declines with age), caloric restriction, fasting, and compounds like resveratrol and NMN. SIRT1 (the most studied) deacetylates histones to silence genes, activates autophagy, and promotes mitochondrial biogenesis. The Sinclair lab's 'Information Theory of Aging' proposes that aging is driven by loss of epigenetic information, and sirtuins are the primary repair system for this information.
keyPoints: 7 sirtuins (SIRT1-7), each with different locations and functions
Require NAD+ as a cofactor — activity declines as NAD+ falls with age
SIRT1 is activated by resveratrol and caloric restriction
David Sinclair's research links sirtuin activation to lifespan extension

title: Epigenetics
summary: How lifestyle and environment change which genes are expressed — without changing the DNA sequence itself.
body: Epigenetics refers to changes in gene expression that don't involve alterations to the underlying DNA sequence. These changes are mediated by chemical modifications to DNA (methylation) and the proteins around which DNA is wrapped (histones). Crucially, epigenetic patterns are influenced by diet, exercise, stress, sleep, and environmental exposures — meaning your lifestyle actively changes how your genes behave. Biological age (measured by epigenetic clocks like the Horvath clock) can differ significantly from chronological age, and lifestyle interventions can reverse epigenetic aging. The 'epigenetic noise' theory of aging proposes that accumulated epigenetic errors drive aging, not just DNA mutations.
keyPoints: DNA methylation patterns are the primary epigenetic mechanism studied for aging
Biological age (epigenetic age) can be measured and reversed
Exercise, diet, and sleep measurably change epigenetic patterns
Identical twins diverge epigenetically over time based on lifestyle

title: Blood Glucose Regulation
summary: How your body maintains stable blood sugar — and why glucose spikes matter for energy, aging, and disease risk.
body: Blood glucose regulation is the process by which your body maintains blood sugar within a tight range (70–100 mg/dL fasting). After eating carbohydrates, glucose enters the bloodstream and the pancreas releases insulin to shuttle it into cells. Frequent large glucose spikes drive chronic insulin elevation, which over time leads to insulin resistance, fat accumulation, and metabolic disease. Even in non-diabetics, continuous glucose monitoring studies show significant glucose variability that correlates with energy levels, mood, and cognitive performance. Strategies to reduce glucose spikes include eating fiber and protein before carbohydrates, walking after meals, apple cider vinegar, and berberine.
keyPoints: Fasting glucose >100 mg/dL indicates prediabetes
Post-meal spikes above 140 mg/dL cause glycation (protein damage)
Walking 10 min after eating reduces glucose spikes by ~30%
Fiber eaten first significantly blunts carbohydrate absorption

title: Gut-Brain Axis
summary: The bidirectional communication highway between your gut microbiome and your brain — influencing mood, cognition, and behavior.
body: The gut-brain axis is a complex bidirectional communication system linking the enteric nervous system (the gut's own nervous system, with 500 million neurons) with the central nervous system via the vagus nerve, the immune system, and the bloodstream. Gut bacteria produce and regulate neurotransmitters including 90% of the body's serotonin, as well as GABA, dopamine precursors, and short-chain fatty acids that directly affect brain function. Gut dysbiosis (microbial imbalance) is now associated with depression, anxiety, autism spectrum disorder, and neurodegenerative diseases. This is an active and rapidly evolving research area — psychobiotics (probiotics for mental health) are now under serious clinical investigation.
keyPoints: 90% of serotonin is produced in the gut by enterochromaffin cells
Gut bacteria produce GABA, which reduces anxiety
Leaky gut allows bacterial products (LPS) to enter bloodstream and cause neuroinflammation
Fecal microbiota transplants are being studied for depression and anxiety

title: Protein Synthesis & Muscle Protein Synthesis
summary: The process by which your body builds new muscle protein — driven by resistance training and dietary protein.
body: Muscle protein synthesis (MPS) is the process by which the body assembles new protein structures in muscle tissue, driven primarily by resistance training (the anabolic stimulus) and dietary protein (the building material). Leucine is the key amino acid that 'switches on' MPS by activating mTOR. The minimum leucine threshold to maximally stimulate MPS is approximately 2–3g per meal (found in roughly 30–40g of quality protein). After resistance training, the 'anabolic window' for elevated MPS lasts 24–48 hours — the old 30-minute post-workout window has been largely debunked for trained individuals. Total daily protein (1.6–2.2g/kg/day) matters more than protein timing for muscle growth.
keyPoints: Leucine is the key trigger — need ~2–3g per meal to maximally stimulate MPS
Total daily protein (1.6–2.2g/kg) matters more than timing
MPS elevation from training lasts 24–48 hours
Older adults need more protein (2.2–2.6g/kg) due to 'anabolic resistance'

title: Neuroplasticity
summary: The brain's ability to reorganize and form new neural connections throughout life — not fixed after childhood.
body: Neuroplasticity is the brain's capacity to change its structure and function in response to experience, learning, injury, and environment. New neurons are generated in the hippocampus (neurogenesis) throughout adulthood — particularly stimulated by aerobic exercise and BDNF. Synaptic plasticity — the strengthening or weakening of connections between neurons — underlies learning and memory. Key drivers of neuroplasticity include aerobic exercise (raises BDNF, the brain's growth factor), sleep (consolidates memories and clears metabolic waste via the glymphatic system), novel experiences, learning new skills, and certain compounds (lion's mane mushroom, magnesium threonate, omega-3s). Chronic stress, sleep deprivation, and sedentary behavior reduce neuroplasticity.
keyPoints: BDNF (Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor) is the primary driver of neurogenesis
Aerobic exercise is the most potent natural BDNF booster
Sleep is essential for memory consolidation and glymphatic clearance
Lion's mane mushroom stimulates NGF (Nerve Growth Factor)

title: BDNF
summary: Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor — the brain's 'fertilizer' that drives neurogenesis, learning, and mood.
body: BDNF (Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor) is a protein that supports the growth, survival, and differentiation of neurons. Often called 'Miracle-Gro for the brain,' it is essential for neurogenesis, synaptic plasticity, learning, and memory. Low BDNF is associated with depression, cognitive decline, and neurodegeneration. The single most potent way to raise BDNF is aerobic exercise — a single bout of aerobic exercise increases BDNF significantly within minutes. Other BDNF boosters: intermittent fasting, omega-3 DHA, curcumin, lion's mane, magnesium, sunlight, social connection, and learning new skills. Chronic stress, sleep deprivation, excess sugar, and sedentary behavior suppress BDNF.
keyPoints: Aerobic exercise is the strongest natural BDNF stimulus
BDNF declines with chronic stress and sleep deprivation
Low BDNF is a biomarker in depression
DHA (omega-3) is structurally required for BDNF receptor function

title: Glymphatic System
summary: The brain's waste clearance system — active primarily during deep sleep, flushing out metabolic debris including Alzheimer's-linked proteins.
body: The glymphatic system is a network of channels surrounding brain blood vessels that clears metabolic waste from the brain during sleep. Cerebrospinal fluid flows through these channels, flushing out waste products including amyloid-beta and tau proteins — the hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease — along with other metabolic byproducts. The system is approximately 10x more active during sleep than during waking, particularly during slow-wave (deep) sleep. Sleep deprivation dramatically impairs glymphatic clearance. The optimal sleep position for glymphatic drainage appears to be lateral (side sleeping). This discovery (2013, Maiken Nedergaard) fundamentally changed understanding of why we sleep.
keyPoints: 10x more active during sleep vs waking
Clears amyloid-beta and tau (Alzheimer's proteins)
Deep sleep (slow-wave) is the most important phase for glymphatic clearance
Side sleeping optimizes glymphatic drainage

title: Telomeres
summary: Protective caps on chromosomes that shorten with each cell division — a biological clock of aging.
body: Telomeres are repetitive DNA sequences at the ends of chromosomes that protect genetic information during cell division, similar to the plastic tips on shoelaces. With each cell division, telomeres shorten slightly. When they become critically short, cells enter senescence (stop dividing) or apoptosis (die). Telomere length is a marker of biological aging and cellular stress. Telomerase, the enzyme that rebuilds telomeres, is active in stem cells and can be activated by certain lifestyle factors. Lifestyle factors that accelerate telomere shortening include chronic stress, obesity, smoking, sleep deprivation, and sedentary behavior. Factors that preserve or lengthen telomeres include exercise, omega-3s, mindfulness meditation, and social connection.
keyPoints: Telomerase rebuilds telomeres — active in stem cells
Short telomeres = increased cancer and aging risk
Chronic stress accelerates telomere shortening via cortisol
Elizabeth Blackburn won Nobel Prize for telomere discovery (2009)
